choices: Patch the 9.8 immediately: severity scores are the industry standard, and deviating from them creates audit risk.
Patch the 7.2 on the jump host first: it sits on the shortest path to the crown jewels, while the 9.8 sits on a dead-end branch. Path risk outranks raw score.
Patch both at once by skipping testing, since a 9.8 and a 7.2 both demand immediate action.
Patch neither and request budget for a new scanner, because conflicting scores mean the data is unreliable.
evidence: Vulnerability graph

kiosk-04 (lobby): CVE score 9.8, RCE --no outgoing edges--> [dead end]
jump-srv-01: CVE score 7.2, privesc --2 hops--> finance-db  [CROWN JEWEL]
path kiosk-04 -> crown jewel: NONE
Scanner output

CVE-9.8: critical, remote code execution on kiosk-04 (isolated lobby VLAN).
CVE-7.2: high, privilege escalation on jump-srv-01 (admin access to production).
scenarios.hint: Ask which vulnerability an attacker can actually walk from, toward something you care about.
scenarios.prompt: With one patch window, which do you fix first?
scenarios.situation: Patch Tuesday lands two candidates. One is a 9.8 RCE on an isolated lobby kiosk; the other is a 7.2 privilege-escalation flaw on the jump server your admins use daily. Your CISO asks which gets tonight's single maintenance window. Your vulnerability graph shows the kiosk flaw has no outgoing edges to anything valuable, while the jump-server flaw is two hops from the finance database.
scenarios.title: Patch the path, not the score
scenarios.why: Vulnerability graphs beat flat CVE lists because risk is reachability times impact. A critical flaw with no path to anything valuable is a theoretical problem; a merely-high flaw on the shortest path to the crown jewels is an active campaign waiting to happen. This is the central operational lesson of attack-path analysis.

choices: A single alert is enough: any access outside a user's home department should trigger an account lockout.
The graph is overkill: a simple rule on the file server would have caught this just as well.
The user-asset graph flagged an anomalous relationship, a finance clerk suddenly connected to build servers she never touched, which no signature or single-event rule would catch.
The graph proves malicious intent, so the correct response is immediate termination of the employee.
evidence: User-asset graph

user:f.clerk --12 months normal--> [HR systems, payroll, email]
user:f.clerk --NEW, last 3 days--> build-srv-01, build-srv-02 (source repos)
build-srv-01 --unusual--> external:personal-cloud.example (uploads, 2 GB)
Context
f.clerk has valid credentials, passed MFA, and no malware was found on her workstation. Role: payroll clerk, finance department.
scenarios.hint: What is unusual here: any single event, or the pattern of relationships over time?
scenarios.prompt: Why did the graph catch what traditional tooling missed?
scenarios.situation: Your UEBA dashboard flags a payroll clerk. Her credentials are valid, her MFA checks out, and no malware was found. But the user-asset graph shows something new: after twelve months of touching only HR and payroll systems, her node has sprouted edges to the source-code build servers, and one of those servers has started uploading to a personal cloud account.
scenarios.title: The finance clerk and the build servers
scenarios.why: Insiders already have legitimate credentials, so single events look normal. Graph-based anomaly detection compares the structure of relationships against history: a user node acquiring connections far outside its normal scope is the tell. This is UEBA-style detection done relationally, and the graph also gives investigators the consolidated view: which systems she touched, what flowed where, and whether it is malicious or benign.

choices: Evaluate only her role attribute, because relationship-based control is a marketing term for plain RBAC.

Traverse the graph: follow reports_to edges from the user to her manager, follow owns edges from the manager to projects, and check whether the requested resource's project node connects, all during business hours. The policy is a path query.
Ask the user to email her manager for approval, since graphs cannot enforce policy in real time.
Grant access because her credentials are valid: Zero Trust only applies to external users.
evidence: Access request

user:a.reyes requests write access to repo:ledger-core at 14:20 local time
user:a.reyes --reports_to--> mgr:d.okafor
mgr:d.okafor --owns--> project:ledger
epo:ledger-core --belongs to--> project:ledger
Policy
Allow write if the requester reports (directly or transitively) to a manager who owns the resource's project, and the request occurs during business hours.
scenarios.hint: Turn the policy sentence into a walk: user -> manager -> project -> resource. Does the walk exist?
scenarios.prompt: How does the policy engine decide?
scenarios.situation: Your identity team is piloting relationship-based access control (ReBAC) for the engineering org. A developer requests write access to a ledger repository. The written policy says: allow if the requester reports to a manager who owns the resource's project, during business hours. The graph holds the org chart, project ownership, and repo membership as nodes and edges.
scenarios.title: ReBAC in action
scenarios.why: ReBAC policies are path queries on the identity graph: users, managers, projects, and resources are nodes; reports_to and owns are edges; evaluation is a traversal. A graph database answers this in one connected query, whereas a relational design would join many tables, and it re-evaluates continuously: if the manager changes or the device falls out of compliance, the trusted path disappears and sessions can be rechecked instantly.

choices: Document it and move on: application servers sometimes need to talk to HR systems during audits.
Add the edge to the approved baseline so the monitoring stops alerting.
Treat it as a misconfiguration or an intrusion in progress: block or quarantine the unexpected edge, investigate the app server, and only then decide whether the connection was ever legitimate.
Rebuild the entire network immediately: any anomaly means the whole design is compromised.
evidence: Communication graph

app-srv-03 --expected--> db-orders, cache-01
app-srv-03 --UNEXPECTED--> hr-payroll-db (first seen 03:12, no ticket, no change record)
Baseline policy
Approved edges for app-srv-03: db-orders, cache-01. HR segment is a separate microsegment with no approved cross-segment edges.
scenarios.hint: Under 'assume breach', what is the safest default treatment of an unapproved cross-segment edge?
scenarios.prompt: What is the right response?
scenarios.situation: You are rolling out microsegmentation built from the communication graph: clusters of systems that naturally talk to each other become segments, and the choke points between them get enforcement. At 03:12 the graph shows a new edge: an application server connecting to the HR payroll database, a different segment, with no change ticket and no approved baseline entry.
scenarios.title: The edge that should not exist
scenarios.why: Microsegmentation is graph enforcement: approved edges are allow-listed, everything else is suspect by default. Under Zero Trust's assume-breach posture, an unexpected cross-segment connection is treated as misconfiguration or malicious until proven otherwise: contain first, investigate, then either approve it as a legitimate new dependency or remove it. The graph makes the violation visible the moment it appears.

choices: Isolate the workstation first: it is the known-compromised node and the pivot point with edges into both the file server and dozens of alerts. Then work outward along the graph, re-imaging each connected node before it is cleared.
Reimage the file server first: it holds the most data, so it must be the attacker's real target.
Wipe everything at once: with lateral movement confirmed, surgical containment is too slow.
Monitor for another day: the graph is still incomplete, and acting on partial data risks disrupting the business.
evidence: Incident graph

ws-07 [CONFIRMED compromised] --SMB--> fileserver-02
ws-07 --RDP--> ws-11, ws-14
fileserver-02 --50 shared alerts--> malware-hash:H
ws-07: first-seen C2 beaconing 01:40
War-room status
CFO on the bridge. Business impact of isolating ws-07: one user offline. Business impact of isolating fileserver-02: 400 users offline.
scenarios.hint: Which node, if isolated, severs the most attack movement for the least business cost?
scenarios.prompt: What containment order does the graph support?
scenarios.situation: 1:40 AM: the SOC confirms a workstation is beaconing to a command-and-control server. The incident graph shows the workstation with SMB and RDP edges into a file server and two more workstations, and the file server shares alerts with dozens of other hosts through a common malware hash. The CFO is on the bridge asking for the plan.
scenarios.title: Blast radius at 1:40 AM
scenarios.why: The graph is the blast-radius map: it shows how far the attacker likely got and which connections they leveraged. Isolating the confirmed pivot (the workstation) first severs the most movement for the least business cost, then responders clear outward along the edges. This is also why the war-room graph works as a shared picture: technical responders and the CFO see the same incident map, and every severed link documents the response in real time.

choices: It replaces analysts: once trained, the model can autonomously delete any node it labels malicious.
It is only useful for marketing: centrality is a vanity metric with no security meaning.

The model learns connection patterns across entities (which node and subgraph shapes look like attacks), and graph features like centrality become inputs that raise an alert's priority when it comes from a highly connected endpoint.
It proves that signature-based detection is obsolete and should be uninstalled.
evidence: Model card

Graph neural network trained on labeled subgraphs of network/entity behavior.
Features per node: degree, betweenness centrality, community membership.
Output: node/subgraph classified attack vs normal.
SOC observation
An alert from a highly central endpoint (connected to many critical systems) is now auto-prioritized; a structurally similar alert from an isolated kiosk is not.
scenarios.hint: What can a model see in the graph's shape that a flat event stream cannot?
scenarios.prompt: What does graph machine learning actually add to detection?
scenarios.situation: Your team is evaluating a graph-neural-network pilot. The vendor claims it 'learns attacks from the graph'. Your CISO asks you to explain, in plain terms, what the model does that your existing rules do not, and what role plain graph metrics play in it.
scenarios.title: AI meets the graph
scenarios.why: Graphs give machine learning rich structural features: centrality, community membership, and subgraph shapes. A graph neural network can learn which connection patterns look like attacks (for example, node classification of IP-port nodes into ATT&CK tactic sources), catching multi-entity correlations that rules miss. Plain graph metrics still earn their keep as features and as priority signals: an alert on a central node deserves more attention than the same alert on an isolated one.

choices: Buy the most expensive enterprise platform immediately: small teams need the biggest tool to compensate.
Patch everything equally: with limited staff, fairness across systems is the defensible strategy.

Run a mini attack-graph analysis to find the critical paths, then fix the small set of weaknesses that cuts the most risk; automate the recurring graph queries (stale access, unknown devices) that a larger team would do by hand.
Outsource everything and skip the analysis: graphs are an enterprise luxury.
evidence: Environment

38 employees, one IT generalist, cloud SaaS plus two on-prem servers.
Attack-graph pilot: 5 specific fixes (2 patches, 2 config changes, 1 segmentation rule) cut 80% of modeled paths to the customer database.
Constraint
Security budget: one afternoon a week. No dedicated SOC.
scenarios.hint: If you can only fix five things, how do you pick the right five?
scenarios.prompt: What is the highest-leverage first move?
scenarios.situation: You advise a 38-person company with one IT generalist and one afternoon a week for security. A quick attack-graph pilot reveals that five specific fixes would eliminate most modeled paths to their customer database, and routine questions like 'does any ex-employee still have access to anything?' are answerable with simple graph queries.
scenarios.title: The SMB force multiplier
scenarios.why: For resource-constrained teams, the graph is a force multiplier: it concentrates scarce effort on the choke points that matter instead of spreading it evenly, and it automates the correlation work a large SOC team would do manually. A single pane showing which systems connect to the infected node, or which five fixes cut most attack paths, is the difference between a contained incident and a breach that closes the business.

choices: Show the spreadsheet of all 4,000 vulnerabilities: executives love raw data.
Show nothing until the incident is fully resolved: partial information is worse than none.
Show the SIEM query syntax: technical credibility impresses leadership.
Show the graph: one picture of the affected nodes, the attacker's path, and the severed containment links. It communicates interconnected risk where a spreadsheet overwhelms.
evidence: Audience
Board member: 'Explain the incident in two minutes. What is exposed, what did you do, and are we safe?'
Materials available
Incident graph: compromised nodes marked, attack path highlighted, containment actions shown as severed edges. Raw alternative: 4,000-row vulnerability export.
scenarios.hint: Which format lets a non-technical leader see the story in two minutes?
scenarios.prompt: How do you brief the board?
scenarios.situation: The incident is contained. A board member asks for a two-minute explanation: what was exposed, what you did, and whether the company is safe. You have the live incident graph and a 4,000-row vulnerability spreadsheet. You have one slide.
scenarios.title: The war-room picture
scenarios.why: Graph visualization is a communication tool, not just an analyst tool: the same picture that guided containment briefs executives and cross-functional teams. Where a spreadsheet of vulnerabilities confuses, a network diagram tells the story of what was at risk, how the attacker moved, and what was cut. Engaging leadership with visual risk is also how security wins budget for the next segmentation project.

key_points: A graph is nodes (things: users, hosts, IPs, domains, hashes) joined by edges (relationships: logged into, resolved to, downloaded).
Link analysis predates computers: Euler's 1736 bridge puzzle founded graph theory; investigators charted criminal networks on paper long before software did it for them.
An attack graph maps every path an attacker could chain through your systems and flaws to reach your crown jewels.
Threat-intel knowledge graphs turn isolated indicators into connected campaigns by linking shared infrastructure.
domains.name: Security Graphs: Think Like an Attacker
domains.summary: Foundations of graph thinking in security: nodes, edges, and link analysis from Euler to modern security operations. Learn to read attack graphs, map kill chains, and pivot through threat-intel knowledge graphs the way an attacker maps your network.

choices: The edges are the relationships, and they are what make the graph useful: 'logged into' and 'resolved to' came from evidence and are where an attacker's movement shows up.
The nodes matter most; edges are just drawing lines to make the diagram pretty and can be ignored when prioritizing work.
A graph like this is equivalent to a spreadsheet with the same four rows; visualization adds no analytical value.
Direction on the edges is irrelevant: 'downloaded from' and 'downloaded to' mean the same thing for investigations.
evidence: Graph excerpt

user:j.doe --logged into--> host:ws-07
host:ws-07 --downloaded--> file:invoice.exe
domain:evil.example.com --resolved to--> ip:93.184.x.x
file:invoice.exe --downloaded from--> domain:evil.example.com
Analyst note
All four nodes are real things we observed. The labeled lines came from logs: auth logs, DNS logs, and the endpoint agent. Nothing here is decorative.
scenarios.hint: Ask yourself which part of the diagram came from the logs, and which part an attacker would have to walk along.
scenarios.prompt: Which statement about this graph is correct?
scenarios.situation: You are shadowing a SOC analyst who pulls up an investigation graph after a suspicious download alert. The graph shows a workstation node, a user node, a domain node, and a file-hash node, all joined by labeled lines. She asks you to sanity-check her interpretation of the model before she briefs the shift lead.
scenarios.title: Reading a security graph
scenarios.why: Edges carry the relationship semantics: who touched what, what resolved to what. Attackers move along relationships (logins, DNS resolutions, downloads), so the edges are the terrain you defend. Direction matters because 'A downloaded from B' and 'A sent data to B' are different facts. As Dr. Chase Cunningham puts it in Think Like an Attacker (2025): 'See the connections. Defend the future.'

choices: Link analysis was invented for the War on Terror and has no earlier history in mathematics or law enforcement.

Euler 1736 (graph theory) -> 1970s paper link charts (Anacapa era) -> 1990s analyst software -> post-9/11 large-scale 'connecting the dots' -> commercial graph algorithms like PageRank running in parallel.
Graph theory began with PageRank in 1998; everything before that was unrelated military work.
Analyst's Notebook created link analysis in the 1990s; earlier investigators used only gut instinct and paper files.
evidence: Timeline reference

1736: Euler models Konigsberg's land masses as nodes and bridges as links, founding graph theory.
1975: Anacapa-style link charts give investigators a systematic paper method for mapping people, organizations, and properties.
1990s: tools like Analyst's Notebook partially automate chart creation.
Post-2001: 'connecting the dots' drives heavy investment in graph-based intelligence analysis.
Commercial echoes

Late 1990s: PageRank treats the web as a graph of pages and links.
2000s: social platforms build businesses on the 'social graph' of people-to-people connections.
scenarios.hint: Which option starts in the 1700s and includes both the paper-chart era and the post-2001 era?
scenarios.prompt: Which lineage is historically accurate?
scenarios.situation: During a team lunch-and-learn you are asked to give the two-minute history of link analysis in security. A junior teammate thinks 'connecting the dots' started with modern SIEMs. You know the lineage runs deeper, from an 18th-century math puzzle to paper charts used by 1970s investigators to the post-2001 intelligence push.
scenarios.title: From Euler to the SOC
scenarios.why: The lineage is real and verifiable: Euler formalized node-link modeling in 1736 with the Konigsberg bridge puzzle; law-enforcement link charts (the Anacapa tradition, mid-1970s) systematized it on paper; analyst software mechanized it in the 1990s; and after 2001 the intelligence community scaled it up to find joined-up pictures in communications and financial records. Meanwhile PageRank and social graphs proved the same math at internet scale.

choices: Fix the printer branch first, since dead-end branches are the easiest wins.
Patch the VPN gateway's RCE flaw and force credential resets on the file server: these two nodes sit on the only complete path to the crown jewel, so breaking that path neutralizes the campaign.
Patch nothing and monitor, because a path of length 3 is too long for a real attacker to complete.
Focus only on the database: if the crown jewel is hardened, the rest of the graph does not matter.
evidence: Attack graph

attacker(external) --exploit RCE--> vpn-gateway
vpn-gateway --reuse weak creds--> file-server
file-server --query with svc account--> customer-db  [CROWN JEWEL]
vpn-gateway --spoof--> printer  [dead end: no further edges]
Window constraint
Two changes tonight: patching the gateway's RCE flaw counts as one, forcing credential resets on the file server counts as one, segmenting the gateway counts as one.
scenarios.hint: Count the hops to the crown jewel on each branch. Which branch actually arrives anywhere?
scenarios.prompt: What does the graph tell you to do?
scenarios.situation: Your vulnerability scanner finished overnight. The attack-graph tooling turned the results into a map: an external attacker node, a VPN gateway with an unpatched remote-code flaw, a file server with weak credentials, and your customer database. A printer also hangs off the gateway as a side branch. You have one maintenance window tonight and can only fix or isolate two things.
scenarios.title: Trace the path to the crown jewels
scenarios.why: The graph shows one complete chain (length 3) to the database and one dead-end branch. Breaking any edge on the complete chain kills the campaign, and the gateway is the choke point both branches share. This is path-based prioritization: you defend the path, not individual nodes in isolation.

choices: It does not: three mediums are still three mediums, and the graph is just a prettier dashboard.

The graph connects the three events through shared entities and time into one kill-chain subgraph (credential access -> lateral movement -> exfiltration), revealing a coordinated intrusion that the flat alert list hid.
The graph proves the alerts are false positives because no single alert reached high severity.
The graph shows the attacker skipped weaponization, which is impossible, so the data must be wrong.
evidence: Alert chain

02:14 failed logins x40 -> host:ws-07
02:26 successful admin login -> server:fileserver-02 (same source IP as the failed logins)
02:41 large outbound transfer -> host:fileserver-02 to external ip (first-seen destination)
MITRE mapping

failed logins -> credential access attempt
admin login on new host -> lateral movement
large outbound transfer -> exfiltration (actions on objectives)
scenarios.hint: List what each alert is in kill-chain terms, then check whether they connect through shared hosts, IPs, and time.
scenarios.prompt: Why does the graph view change the assessment?
scenarios.situation: Your SOC queue shows three alerts from last night: a failed-login spike on a workstation, a successful admin login on a server ten minutes later, and an unusual outbound transfer from a database shortly after. Each alert alone scored medium. None of them fired a high-severity rule. You pull them into the security graph.
scenarios.title: Three alerts, one campaign
scenarios.why: Correlating disparate alerts onto one graph by shared entities and sequence is exactly how defenders reconstruct kill chains. Each event is weak alone; together they form the credential-theft -> lateral-movement -> exfiltration pattern. This is also why attack frameworks like MITRE ATT&CK can be codified as subgraphs: when that relationship pattern appears in live data, the system can flag the campaign, not just the events.

choices: None: the feed said unknown, so the domain must be treated as benign until the vendor updates.

The shared-infrastructure edge links the unknown domain to a known phishing campaign in one hop, letting you enrich the alert, block the IP, and hunt for other victims before the vendor feed ever catches up.
It proves the endpoint agent was wrong, because feeds are always more accurate than local graphs.
It proves attribution to a specific actor, which is all you need for the incident report.
evidence: Knowledge graph pivot

domain:new-bad.example --resolved to--> ip:93.184.x.x
ip:93.184.x.x --also hosted--> domain:phish-finance-1.example [known campaign FIN-PHISH]
ip:93.184.x.x --also hosted--> domain:phish-finance-2.example [known campaign FIN-PHISH]
Feed status
Vendor feed verdict on new-bad.example: UNKNOWN (no reputation).
scenarios.hint: What does the unknown domain share with things you already know are bad?
scenarios.prompt: What is the graph's investigative value here?
scenarios.situation: An endpoint agent flags a download from a domain your team has never seen. The threat-intel feed lists it as 'unknown'. Your knowledge graph, however, has that domain node already: it resolved to an IP last week that also hosted two domains tied to a known phishing campaign against finance teams.
scenarios.title: Pivoting the threat-intel graph
scenarios.why: Threat-intel knowledge graphs model indicators (IPs, domains, hashes) as nodes linked to campaigns and actors. Pivoting across those edges enriches alerts with context no single feed provides: the unknown domain inherits suspicion from its shared infrastructure. Attribution still needs more than one shared IP, but enrichment and hunting can start immediately.

choices: The database: it holds the data, so protecting it directly is always the top priority regardless of paths.
The print server: it is the cheapest to harden, maximizing return on limited budget.
The jump server: it is the highest-centrality node on the attack graph, a choke point on every path, so hardening it degrades all four attacker routes at once.
The web server: attackers always start at the web tier, so it must be the most important node.
evidence: Centrality table

jump-srv-01: on 4 of 4 attack paths (betweenness: highest)
web-01: on 2 of 4 attack paths
db-01: on 3 of 4 paths but unreachable without passing jump-srv-01
printer-03: on 0 paths
Constraint
Budget covers hardening exactly one system this quarter.
scenarios.hint: If you could remove one node from the graph, which removal breaks the most paths to the crown jewels?
scenarios.prompt: Which system do you harden, and what principle guides the choice?
scenarios.situation: The red team hands you their path analysis: four possible routes into the network, and you can only harden one system this quarter. The graph metrics are computed for every host. One host, a jump server, sits on all four attack paths; the web server sits on two; the print server sits on none.
scenarios.title: Centrality finds the choke point
scenarios.why: Centrality (here, betweenness on attack paths) measures how much attacker traffic must flow through a node. Hardening the choke point that every path shares is the highest-leverage single move: it degrades all four campaigns, while hardening an endpoint node only degrades the paths that include it. 'Think like the attacker' means finding the node they cannot avoid.

choices: Do nothing: the database is patched and hardened, so the exposure is acceptable.
Remove or correct the NAT rule immediately: the graph revealed that the crown jewel is one hop from the internet, and that edge is the risk regardless of the database's patch state.
Patch the database again to be safe, then schedule a firewall review for next quarter.
Delete the graph: if the CMDB does not show the rule, the rule probably does not exist.
evidence: Graph excerpt

internet --NAT rule #447 (forgotten)--> db-01
internet --(no edge)--> web-01  [properly tiered, WAF in front]
db-01 status
Patched, strong credentials, encrypted at rest. The NAT rule predates the current firewall admin and is undocumented.
scenarios.hint: Which is easier for an attacker: cracking a hardened database, or walking through an open door?
scenarios.prompt: What is the right response?
scenarios.situation: You build your first living asset graph from scan data and firewall configs. Zooming into the database segment, you see something the CMDB never showed: the customer database is exactly one hop from the internet through a forgotten NAT rule on an old firewall. The database itself is fully patched and the passwords are strong.
scenarios.title: The one-hop problem
scenarios.why: This is the classic graph insight: a relationship (the forgotten NAT rule) creates risk that no amount of node hardening removes. The database can be perfectly patched and still be one exploit or misconfig away from the internet. Graphs make such one-hop exposures visible where tables and inventories hide them; the fix is to break the edge.

concepts: Never trust, always verify: every access decision is re-evaluated, even inside the network.
Microsegmentation: approved communication edges are allow-listed; unexpected edges are treated as hostile.
ReBAC (relationship-based access control): policies expressed as paths on the identity graph (reports_to, owns, member_of).
Continuous verification: device health, location, and behavior are edges that can change, revoking trust live.
Anomalous edge detection: a brand-new connection between nodes that never talked is the classic breach signal.

example.code:
# relationship-based policy as a graph walk (pseudocode)
user:a.reyes -[:reports_to]-> mgr:d.okafor -[:owns]-> project:ledger
repo:ledger-core -[:belongs_to]-> project:ledger
# ALLOW write iff a continuous path user -> ... -> resource exists
# AND device node is marked compliant AND time is business hours
# device falls out of compliance -> trusted edge removed -> session rechecked
example.walkthrough: The policy is a path query: does a continuous chain of relationships connect this user to this resource through the owning manager and project? Two more conditions ride on other edges: the device's compliance status and the time window. If the device node flips to non-compliant, the trusted edge disappears and the session is re-evaluated immediately. That is continuous verification made concrete.

pitfalls: Trusting yesterday's graph: a device that was compliant at 9 AM may not be at 2 PM; stale edges are how attackers persist.
Coarse network rules: allowing a whole subnet because one host needs access recreates the flat network Zero Trust was meant to kill.
Building the identity graph but never querying it: the graph only enforces Zero Trust when policy engines traverse it on every decision.
lessons.title: Zero Trust runs on relationships
lessons.try_it: Write one access rule for your own lab as a relationship sentence: 'Allow X to reach Y if ...' Then list the exact nodes and edges the rule would need (user, device, project, time). Could you evaluate it by walking a graph? Where would the walk fail today?

concepts: Node: any entity worth tracking (user, host, IP, domain, file hash, vulnerability).
Edge: a labeled relationship between two nodes (logged into, resolved to, downloaded).
Directed vs undirected edges: direction changes the meaning of an attack path.
Degree and centrality: how connected a node is; high-centrality nodes are attacker highways.
Security graph: the living model of your environment as nodes and edges.
Attack graph: the subset of the security graph showing how flaws chain into paths to targets.

example.code:
# a security graph written as an adjacency list
ws-07  --logged into-->  j.doe
ws-07  --downloaded-->    invoice.exe
invoice.exe --came from--> evil.example.com
# degree(ws-07) = 2, degree(invoice.exe) = 2
# remove the edge to evil.example.com -> the download path breaks
example.walkthrough: This tiny adjacency list is a complete security graph: four nodes, three labeled edges. The degree count shows which entities touch the most activity. Deleting one edge (blocking the domain) breaks the attacker's path without touching the user's workstation. That is the core move you will repeat at enterprise scale: edit the graph, not just the node.

pitfalls: Treating edges as decoration: the labels (logged into, resolved to) carry the investigative meaning, not the circles.
Confusing a graph with a chart: a chart displays data; a graph is a queryable model you can traverse, measure, and update.
Assuming all connections are equal: an edge from the internet to a database and an edge between two printers are different risks.
lessons.title: Nodes, edges, and the attacker's map
lessons.try_it: Sketch your home network as a graph on paper: router, laptop, phone, smart TV as nodes; draw and label every edge (Wi-Fi association, logins, shared drives). Circle the node with the highest degree and ask: if an attacker owned it, what could they reach in two hops?

concepts: Crown jewels: the assets whose compromise hurts most (customer data, finance systems, source code).
Exploit edge: a vulnerability or misconfiguration that lets an attacker step from one node to the next.
Shortest attack path: the fewest edges between an attacker and a crown jewel.
Path-breaking remediation: removing or guarding one edge/node to sever every path through it.
ATT&CK as subgraphs: attacker tactics codified as relationship patterns to hunt for in live data.

example.code:
$ cat path-to-db.txt
attacker --exploit RCE--> vpn-gateway
vpn-gateway --weak creds--> file-server
file-server --svc account--> customer-db   [CROWN JEWEL]
$ # path length: 3. choke point: vpn-gateway (every path crosses it)
$ # action: patch gateway + rotate file-server creds -> path length: none
example.walkthrough: The text file lists one complete chain of three edges. The walkthrough shows how to read it: count the hops, find the node every path crosses (the choke point), then act on the choke point. Patching the gateway alone breaks this campaign; patching the database alone leaves the attacker two steps away on the next flaw.

pitfalls: Patching by CVSS score alone: a 9.8 with no path to anything valuable is less urgent than a 7.2 on the only road to the database.
Forgetting misconfigurations: an open firewall rule or a forgotten trust relationship is an exploit edge too.
Treating the graph as a one-time project: every scan, deploy, and config change redraws the map.

lessons.title: Graph Theory for Security Practitioners
concepts: A graph is nodes (entities) + edges (relationships) — computers, users, and permissions become a traversable map
Directed vs. undirected: 'User A can access Server B' is directed (A→B); 'Host X communicated with Host Y' may be undirected
Pathfinding algorithms (BFS, DFS, Dijkstra) find attack paths — the routes an attacker could take to reach critical assets
Centrality measures identify high-value targets: which nodes, if compromised, give attackers the most access?

example.code:
Simple AD graph:
  (Alice:User)-[MemberOf]->(Admins:Group)-[AdminTo]->(DC:Computer)
  
  Path: Alice → Admins → DC
  Meaning: Compromise Alice, get Domain Admin via group membership
example.walkthrough: This three-hop path is invisible in a user list but obvious in a graph. Attackers think in graphs — defenders must too.

pitfalls: Treating assets in isolation — a 'low-risk' workstation with a path to DA is high-risk
Ignoring transitive relationships — Alice isn't admin, but Alice→Group→Admin means effective admin
Static analysis only — graphs change; continuous mapping catches new paths
lessons.try_it: Draw a graph of your AD: users → groups → computers. Find the shortest path from a standard user to Domain Admin.

lessons.title: BloodHound and AD Attack Paths
concepts: BloodHound maps Active Directory relationships and finds attack paths to high-value targets automatically
Key edges: MemberOf, AdminTo, CanRDP, DCSync, GenericAll — each represents a potential attacker step
Shortest path analysis answers: 'If I compromise this user, how do I get to Domain Admin?'
Defensive use: find and eliminate unnecessary attack paths before attackers exploit them

example.code:
BloodHound query: Find shortest path to Domain Admins
  MATCH p=shortestPath((u:User)-[*1..]->(g:Group {name:'DOMAIN ADMINS@corp.local'}))
  RETURN p
  
  Result: 4 paths found, shortest is 3 hops via HelpDesk group
example.walkthrough: That HelpDesk group with 'Reset Password' on an admin's account is a 3-hop path to domain compromise. Remove the edge, break the path.

pitfalls: Running BloodHound without permission — it's an offensive tool; get authorization first
Collecting but not acting — finding paths without remediating is just documenting your vulnerabilities
One-time scans — AD changes daily; new paths appear with every permission change
lessons.try_it: If authorized, run BloodHound in your lab. Find the top 3 shortest paths to Domain Admins and propose remediations.

lessons.title: Nodes, Edges, and Properties
concepts: Nodes represent entities: users, computers, IP addresses, files, processes — anything you want to track
Edges represent relationships: 'authenticated to', 'communicated with', 'created process' — the connections between entities
Properties enrich both: nodes have attributes (OS version, last logon), edges have metadata (timestamp, protocol, bytes)
Property graphs (like Neo4j) are the standard for security — they handle rich metadata better than RDF triples

example.code:
Security event as graph:
  (192.168.1.50:IP)-[RESOLVED]->(evil.com:Domain)
  (evil.com:Domain)-[CONNECTED {port:443, bytes:2MB}]->(Workstation:Host)
  (Workstation:Host)-[RAN]->(powershell.exe:Process)
  
  Pattern: DNS → C2 connection → suspicious process = likely compromise
example.walkthrough: This pattern is hard to see in log lines but obvious as a graph. The relationships TELL the story.

pitfalls: Flat log analysis only — missing the connections that reveal attack patterns
Too many node types — start simple (5-10 types), expand as needed
No time properties — when things happened matters as much as what happened
lessons.try_it: Model a phishing attack as a graph: email → user → URL → download → execution. Define the nodes, edges, and key properties.

lessons.title: Crown Jewel Analysis
concepts: Crown jewels are your most critical assets — the things attackers want: domain controllers, backup systems, customer databases
Work backwards from crown jewels: what paths lead here? Which are shortest? Which are least monitored?
Choke points are nodes that many attack paths traverse — defending these gives maximum coverage
Attack path management is continuous: new vulnerabilities, new permissions, and new assets create new paths

example.code:
Crown jewel: Customer database
  Paths in:
    1. Web app → SQL injection → database (3 hops, internet-facing)
    2. Phish user → VPN → internal → database (4 hops)
    3. Vendor access → jump host → database (3 hops, third-party risk)
  
  Choke point: The jump host appears in paths 2 and 3 — harden it first.
example.walkthrough: Path 1 is shortest AND internet-facing — highest priority. But don't ignore path 3: vendor access is often less monitored.

pitfalls: Focusing only on external paths — insider threats and supply chain are real attack vectors
One-time assessment — attack paths change with every patch, permission, and new system
Ignoring path length — shorter paths are easier for attackers; prioritize accordingly
lessons.try_it: Identify your top 3 crown jewels. For each, map the 3 shortest attack paths and identify choke points.

lessons.title: Privilege Escalation Paths
concepts: Most AD compromises follow privilege escalation paths — standard user → local admin → domain admin
Common edges: Kerberoasting (crackable service accounts), AS-REP roasting (no pre-auth), unconstrained delegation
BloodHound's 'Find all Domain Admins' is step one; 'Shortest path from owned principal' is step two
Defensive priority: eliminate paths, don't just patch endpoints — a patched server with a delegation path is still vulnerable

example.code:
Typical escalation chain:
  Standard User
    → (GenericWrite on Service Account) → Change password
    → (Service Account has AdminTo on Server) → Local admin
    → (Server has session for Domain Admin) → Token theft
    → Domain Admin
  
  4 hops. Each edge is a misconfiguration to fix.
example.walkthrough: Every edge is a fixable misconfiguration. GenericWrite shouldn't be there. The service account shouldn't be admin. Sessions shouldn't persist. Fix the graph, not just the endpoints.

pitfalls: Patching without path analysis — the vulnerability is fixed but the attack path remains via another route
Ignoring service accounts — they're often over-privileged and have crackable passwords
No regular path audits — permissions drift; today's secure AD is tomorrow's attack graph
lessons.try_it: Map a privilege escalation path in your lab AD. For each hop, identify the misconfiguration and the remediation.

lessons.title: Cloud Attack Surface Mapping
concepts: Cloud attack graphs map: identities → roles → resources → data — the full blast radius of a compromise
Key cloud edges: AssumeRole, PassRole, IAM policy attachments, security group rules, trust relationships
Cross-account paths are critical — a dev account compromise leading to prod is a common real-world scenario
Tools: CloudMapper, Cartography, native CSPM — continuous mapping, not point-in-time

example.code:
AWS attack path:
  (DevUser)-[AssumeRole]->(DevRole)-[PassRole]->(EC2Instance)
  (EC2Instance)-[InstanceProfile]->(ProdReadRole)
  (ProdReadRole)-[s3:GetObject]->(CustomerDataBucket)
  
  Dev user → customer data in 4 hops via role chaining.
example.walkthrough: The instance profile is the bridge. If that EC2 is compromised, the attacker inherits ProdReadRole. Least privilege on instance profiles breaks this chain.

pitfalls: Ignoring cross-account trust — the dev/prod boundary is only as strong as the trust policy
Overly broad instance profiles — EC2s don't need prod data access 'just in case'
No cloud graph at all — you can't defend what you can't see
lessons.try_it: Map your cloud IAM as a graph. Find the shortest path from a developer identity to production data.

lessons.title: Blast Radius Prioritization
concepts: Not all vulnerabilities are equal — a critical CVE on an isolated test box matters less than a medium CVE on a domain controller
Blast radius = what an attacker gains by exploiting this: which assets become reachable? What privileges?
Graph-based prioritization: rank fixes by (nodes reachable × asset criticality) / remediation effort
This beats CVSS-only prioritization — context matters more than the score

example.code:
Two vulnerabilities:
  A: CVSS 9.8 on isolated IoT device (blast radius: 1 device)
  B: CVSS 7.5 on jump host with paths to 50 servers (blast radius: 50 servers)
  
  Fix B first. CVSS lies; graphs tell the truth.
example.walkthrough: The jump host is a choke point — compromising it unlocks 50 servers. The IoT device is a dead end. Prioritize by graph impact.

pitfalls: CVSS-only prioritization — wastes effort on high-score, low-impact issues
Ignoring asset criticality — a path to the backup server matters more than a path to a printer
No re-assessment — after fixing B, re-run the graph; new choke points emerge
lessons.try_it: Take your top 10 vulnerabilities. Map each to the asset graph. Re-rank by blast radius and compare to CVSS order.

lessons.title: Vulnerability Management: Integration and Interoperability
concepts: Vulnerability Management rarely operates in isolation — integration with other systems is where real-world complexity lives.
API design for Vulnerability Management: version your interfaces, document contracts, handle failures gracefully.
Data format choices matter: JSON for readability, Protocol Buffers for performance, each has tradeoffs.
Idempotency: operations that may be retried must be safe to execute multiple times.

example.code:
Integration patterns:
  Sync (REST/gRPC): Simple, but couples availability
  Async (Queue/Events): Decoupled, but eventual consistency
  Batch (ETL): Efficient for bulk, but high latency
  
  Choose based on: latency requirements, coupling tolerance, failure handling.

pitfalls: Tight coupling — synchronous calls to unreliable dependencies cascade failures.

lessons.title: Zero Trust Architecture: Advanced Patterns and Architectures
concepts: Advanced implementations of Zero Trust Architecture follow established architectural patterns — learn to recognize which pattern fits which problem.
Composition over inheritance: build complex Zero Trust Architecture solutions by combining simple, well-understood components.
The tradeoff triangle: you can optimize for performance, simplicity, or flexibility — pick two. Document which you chose and why.
Refactoring Zero Trust Architecture code: the best time to improve structure is when you understand the domain better, not when you're firefighting.

example.code:
Zero Trust Architecture Architecture:
  ┌─────────────┐
  │   Interface │ ← What users interact with
  ├─────────────┤
  │    Logic    │ ← Core business rules
  ├─────────────┤
  │    Data     │ ← Persistence and state
  └─────────────┘
  Each layer has clear responsibilities and boundaries.
example.walkthrough: Separate concerns into layers. Each layer should be testable independently. When something breaks, the layer structure tells you where to look.

pitfalls: Mixing layers — business logic in the UI layer creates untestable spaghetti.
No clear boundaries — when everything talks to everything, changes cascade unpredictably.
Premature abstraction — don't build frameworks; solve the actual problem first.

lessons.title: Zero Trust Architecture: Performance Optimization and Scaling
concepts: Measure first, optimize second: profile Zero Trust Architecture operations to find actual bottlenecks, not assumed ones.
The most impactful optimizations are often algorithmic (better approach) not micro (faster code).
Caching is the highest-ROI optimization for read-heavy Zero Trust Architecture workloads — but invalidation is the hard part.
Scale horizontally when possible: stateless Zero Trust Architecture components scale linearly; stateful ones need careful design.

example.code:
Optimization workflow:
  1. Baseline: Measure current performance (p50, p95, p99)
  2. Profile: Identify the bottleneck (CPU? I/O? Network?)
  3. Hypothesize: What's the root cause?
  4. Optimize: Change one thing
  5. Measure: Did it improve? By how much?
  6. Repeat or revert
example.walkthrough: Follow this workflow for a real Zero Trust Architecture performance issue. Document the baseline, the change, and the measured improvement. If the change didn't help, revert it — don't accumulate complexity without benefit.

pitfalls: Optimizing without measuring — you can't improve what you don't measure.
Premature optimization — clean code first, fast code when profiling shows it's needed.
Ignoring the 99th percentile — averages hide the worst user experiences.

simulations.title: Patch the path, not the CVE score
simulations.brief: Two critical CVEs, one maintenance window. CVE-A scores 9.8 on a print server; CVE-B scores 7.2 on a jump host one hop from the finance database. The attack graph says only one of them matters this week. Decide.

steps.symptom: CVE-A (9.8): print server, no path to crown jewels (isolated VLAN, no trust edges). CVE-B (7.2): jump host with an active session edge to FIN-DB and an RDP edge from a compromised workstation.
options: Patch CVE-A first — 9.8 outranks 7.2
Patch CVE-B first — the attack graph shows a live 2-hop path from attacker foothold to the finance database; CVE-A has no path to anything valuable
Patch both simultaneously by extending the window
Patch neither and accept the risk
evidence: attack-graph.txt
Path: WS-114(compromised) --RDP--> JUMP-01 --session--> FIN-DB. CVE-B enables privesc on JUMP-01. CVE-A host: degree 1, no edges toward crown jewels.
policy.txt
Patch prioritization: reachable paths to crown jewels outrank raw CVSS. A 9.8 on an island is less urgent than a 7.2 on the bridge.
steps.explain: CVSS measures the vulnerability; the attack graph measures your exposure. Risk is the intersection — a critical bug with no path to value is noise, while a medium bug on the attack path is the incident waiting to happen.

steps.symptom: CVE-B patched. How do you prove the graph-driven choice was right, in terms leadership understands?
options: Report the CVSS scores patched
Show the before/after attack graph: the path to FIN-DB is severed, crown-jewel reachability dropped, and mean-time-to-patch on pathed vulnerabilities improved
Count the number of patches applied
Show the scanner is now green
evidence: graph-diff.txt
Before: 3 distinct paths WS-114 -> FIN-DB. After: 0. Crown-jewel reachable nodes: 14 -> 6.
steps.explain: Graph metrics translate security work into business risk: paths to the crown jewels are the unit of exposure. Fewer paths means less risk, regardless of how many CVEs the scanner counted.

simulations.debrief: Patch by path, not by score. The attack graph turns a 10,000-row vulnerability list into a ranked set of exposures — and every patch should visibly shrink the attacker's map.

simulations.title: The anomalous edges: insider or role change?
simulations.brief: The user-asset graph flags m.alvarez: 14 new edges this week to finance systems she never touched before. Insider threat or legitimate change? Investigate.

steps.symptom: 14 new access edges: FIN-DB, payroll shares, finance file servers. All authenticated, all during business hours, all successful.
options: Insider threat — disable the account immediately
Correlate with the HR graph: check for role-change, transfer, or manager-approved access edges before judging the anomaly
Ignore — business hours means legitimate
The graph is wrong — delete the edges
evidence: hr-graph.txt
m.alvarez transferred to Finance 9 days ago (HR edge: TRANSFER). Manager edge: approved access request REQ-2210 covering FIN-DB and payroll shares, 8 days ago.
peer-graph.txt
Her new peers average 16 finance edges; she has 14. Her edge pattern now matches the finance role cluster.
steps.explain: Anomaly without context is just novelty. The HR graph (transfer + approved request) and the peer-group graph (matching the finance cluster) explain every edge. Graphs convict or acquit together — never read one in isolation.

steps.symptom: Legitimate transfer confirmed. But one edge still bothers you: a 2 AM access to the payroll archive, outside her peers' pattern. Next step?
options: Close the case — the transfer explains everything

Investigate the single unexplained edge: check the session details, source host, and whether the credentials were hers — one anomalous edge inside a legitimate pattern is exactly how real insider cases hide
Disable her account for the 2 AM access
Delete the payroll archive
evidence: session.txt
2 AM session: source host WS-114 (not her laptop), authentication via cached credentials, files copied to USB. Her laptop was offline.
steps.explain: The transfer explained 13 edges; the 14th came from a different host with her cached credentials at 2 AM. Real cases hide inside legitimate noise — the graph found the one edge that did not belong, and the session data confirmed it.

simulations.debrief: User-asset graphs do not detect 'bad people' — they detect edges that do not fit. Correlate across graphs (HR, peer, session) before acting, and remember: the clever insider hides one malicious edge inside a legitimate pattern.

simulations.title: Map the blast radius: workstation compromised
simulations.brief: WS-207 is compromised with domain-user credentials. Before you contain, map what the attacker can reach from here. The graph is your battle map.

steps.symptom: WS-207 (10.4.9.207) compromised. Compromised credential: svc-deploy (local admin on 40 hosts, per the privilege graph).
options: Isolate WS-207 immediately and figure out the rest later
Query the graph first: enumerate all nodes reachable from WS-207 via the svc-deploy credential edges, rank by crown-jewel proximity, then contain in priority order
Reset the svc-deploy password and consider it handled
Reimage WS-207
evidence: blast-radius.txt
Reachable via svc-deploy: 40 hosts incl. BUILD-01 (CI), BACKUP-01, and JUMP-02 (1 hop from FIN-DB). WS-207 alone: 3 reachable nodes. With the credential: 40, including 2 crown-jewel-adjacent.
ir-playbook.txt
Blast-radius mapping precedes containment prioritization: you cannot defend what you have not enumerated. Containment order follows crown-jewel proximity.
steps.explain: The compromised host is the least interesting node — the credential is the weapon. The graph shows the credential reaches 40 hosts including CI and backup infrastructure. Contain the crown-jewel-adjacent nodes first, not just the patient zero.

steps.symptom: Blast radius mapped: 40 hosts, JUMP-02 one hop from FIN-DB. What is the containment order?
options: Alphabetical — work through the list
JUMP-02 and BACKUP-01 first (crown-jewel-adjacent and recovery infrastructure), then BUILD-01 (CI), then the remaining hosts, with the svc-deploy credential rotated network-wide
WS-207 first since it was the entry point
Only contain the hosts showing active beacons
evidence: priority.txt
Containment priority = crown-jewel proximity x infrastructure criticality. Backup infra is contained early: an attacker who owns backups owns your recovery.
steps.explain: Graph-driven containment protects what matters most first: the paths to the crown jewels, then the infrastructure you need to recover (backups, CI), then the long tail. Entry point goes last — it is already known and watched.

simulations.debrief: In incident response the graph answers the only question that matters: from here, where can they go? Map the reachable set, rank by value, contain in that order — and always protect your recovery path.

simulations.title: Draw the microsegments from the graph
simulations.brief: The network is flat: 600 hosts, one broadcast domain. The communication graph shows clear communities. Design the microsegmentation plan the graph is asking for.

steps.symptom: Graph communities: finance cluster (38 hosts, dense internal edges), build/CI cluster (24 hosts), printers/IoT (60 hosts, chatty but isolated), user workstations (rest, sparse inter-edges).
options: One segment per host — maximum security
Segment along the graph communities: finance VLAN, CI VLAN, IoT VLAN, workstation VLAN — cutting the sparse inter-community edges and keeping the dense internal ones
Two segments: servers and everything else
Keep it flat but add a firewall
evidence: communities.txt

Inter-community edges: finance<->workstations 12, ci<->workstations 8, iot<->anything 3. Cutting these edges removes 23 lateral paths while breaking zero legitimate workflows (all inter-community traffic is already proxied).
cost.txt
Per-host microsegmentation: 600 policies to maintain. Community segmentation: 4 segments, 23 edge rules.
steps.explain: The graph already drew the segments — communities are where the traffic naturally clusters. Cutting the sparse inter-community edges removes lateral paths at minimum operational cost. Per-host segmentation is theoretically perfect and practically unmaintainable.

steps.symptom: Segments approved. What validates the design before enforcement?
options: Enforce immediately — the graph is always right
Simulate first: run the proposed policy against 30 days of flow logs in the graph and confirm zero legitimate flows would break, then enforce in monitor mode, then block
Ask users if it will break anything
Enforce on Fridays
evidence: simulation.txt
Policy simulation vs 30d flows: 0 legitimate flows denied, 23 lateral paths removed. Monitor mode 2 weeks: 0 complaints. Then enforced.
steps.explain: Graphs model the past; simulation proves the future. Validate against real flow history, then monitor-mode before block-mode — segmentation that breaks the business gets rolled back and never tried again.

simulations.debrief: Microsegmentation is graph partitioning made physical. Let the communication graph draw the boundaries, validate against history, enforce gradually — and every segment should visibly shrink someone's attack paths.

simulations.title: The vendor's edge to the finance database
simulations.brief: A vendor support account requests a direct edge to FIN-DB 'for troubleshooting.' The Zero Trust policy engine asks you to approve or deny the relationship. Decide from the graph.

steps.symptom: Requested edge: vendor-acct --troubleshoot--> FIN-DB (crown jewel). Vendor history: 2 sessions in 6 months, both to the app tier, never the DB. Contract: app-tier support only.
options: Approve — vendors need to troubleshoot
Deny the direct edge: no business justification, no historical pattern, crown-jewel target. Offer a time-boxed, recorded, approval-gated session through the PAM jump host instead
Approve permanently to avoid future tickets
Deny and block the vendor entirely
evidence: zt-policy.txt
Relationship policies: edges to crown jewels require (1) contractual scope, (2) historical precedent or explicit approval, (3) session recording, (4) time bounds. This request meets zero of four.
graph-history.txt
vendor-acct edges, 6 months: app-web-01 (2 sessions). No DB edges ever.
steps.explain: Zero Trust is a relationship decision, and the graph holds the evidence: no precedent, no contract scope, maximum-value target. Deny the standing edge; offer the gated, temporary, recorded alternative. The business need is met without the permanent risk.

steps.symptom: The vendor escalates: 'our SLA requires direct DB access.' Your final answer?
options: Grant it — the SLA settles it

Hold the denial and counter with the PAM-gated session plus a contract amendment process: if the SLA truly requires it, the requirement gets written, risk-accepted, and re-evaluated — not smuggled through a ticket
Grant it quietly and do not document
Escalate to the CEO
evidence: governance.txt
Crown-jewel access changes require documented risk acceptance by the data owner. Verbal SLA claims do not override.
steps.explain: Access to crown jewels is a governance decision with a named risk owner, not a support-ticket negotiation. The graph made the risk visible; the process makes the decision legitimate.

simulations.debrief: Zero Trust policies are graph edges with conditions. Every requested edge to a crown jewel must earn its place: precedent, contract, recording, time bounds — or it does not exist.

points: Pick ONE problem with a real evidence trail: the symptom, what you measured, the hypothesis you tested
Show the loop: scope, observe, hypothesize, smallest safe change, validate — interviewers score the method, not just the fix
Name the tools (VM build, networking, logs) and the lesson it taught you
Close with the result in concrete terms: what works now that did not before
pitfalls: Choosing a story with no real obstacle (“I Googled it” is not a story)
Skipping validation — saying it worked without proving it
Rambling past two minutes without reaching the result

behavioral.prompt: Tell me about a time you dealt with a frustrated customer or user while something was broken.
points: Lead with empathy and ownership: acknowledge the impact before the technical detail
Show translation: what you told them, in their language, plus the timeline you committed to
Show judgment: the narrow fix you chose and what you refused to do (e.g., disabling the control to clear the symptom)
Close with the relationship outcome, not just the technical one
pitfalls: Badmouthing the customer to sound decisive
Promising a timeline you could not keep
Framing the user as the problem rather than the situation

points: Connect prevention to something concrete: a moment you saw detection arrive too late, or a system you hardened
Tie their model to your instincts: deny-by-default matches how you already think about trust
Show service orientation: the Cyber Hero culture rewards the 2 a.m. helper — give an example of being one
Name one forward-looking reason: Zero Trust, the MSP mission, or the bootcamp community investment
pitfalls: Generic flattery with no specifics about the company
Leading with compensation, title, or location convenience
Claiming expertise in products you have only read about — frame it as studied, not mastered
Staying vague ('I analyzed the data') instead of naming what you connected.
Skipping your own role: what did YOU see that others missed?
No outcome: what changed because you joined the dots?
points: The scattered signals and why nobody had connected them yet
The specific links you drew between them (shared host, time, infrastructure)
What the bigger picture turned out to be and what action it drove
What the experience taught you about investigating
behavioral.prompt: Tell me about a time you connected scattered clues into a bigger picture that others had missed.

pitfalls: Claiming you fixed everything: credibility comes from trade-offs, not heroics.
Hiding the constraint: the limitation is what makes the prioritization story real.
No metric: 'better' needs a before-and-after.
points: The constraint (time, budget, staff) and the size of the backlog
How you decided what mattered most (what was reachable, what was critical)
What you did first and what you deliberately deferred
The measurable result of the prioritization
behavioral.prompt: Describe a time you had to prioritize risks or fixes with limited time or resources. How did you decide what came first?

pitfalls: Reciting jargon to a non-technical audience and calling it communication.
Skipping the audience's reaction: did they actually understand and act?
Making yourself the hero instead of the translator.
points: The technical finding and why it mattered
Who the audience was and what they cared about
How you reframed it (a picture, an analogy, a story)
What decision or action the audience took because they understood
behavioral.prompt: Tell me about a time you explained a complex technical finding to a non-technical audience and it changed a decision.
Tell me about a time you used automation or AI to solve a security problem.
points: The repetitive security task and what it cost in analyst time
The automation or AI approach you built and how you validated it
Measured outcome: time saved, detection gained, false positives changed
pitfalls: Describing the tool but never the validation
No measurable outcome

behavioral.prompt: Describe a time you had to decide whether to trust an automated security decision.
points: The stakes of the automated action and its blast radius
How you verified before acting (or the gate you built)
What happened and what you would automate differently next time
pitfalls: Saying you always trust the tool
No mention of blast radius or reversibility

sections.heading: Product stack
items: Allowlisting — default-deny execution control for apps, DLLs, scripts, installers
Ringfencing — constrains allowed apps: app-to-app, file, registry, network
Storage Control — USB/device policy by serial, user, file type, encryption
Elevation Control — just-in-time per-app admin, no standing rights
Network Control — host firewall; port/IP/dynamic-ACL rules; ZTNA foundation
Web Control — agent-based DNS/URL category filtering, works off-network
Cyber Hero MDR — 24/7/365 US-based response, ~60-second average
Testing Environment — one-button VDI sandbox; checks AV flags, canary files, registry changes

sections.heading: Rule strength (strongest to weakest)
items: Certificate/publisher rules — survive version updates
Hash rules — precise but break on every new version
Path rules — weakest; never in user-writable locations
Learning Mode catalogs before enforcement; Installation Mode pauses blocking — scope and time-box both

sections.heading: Terminal evidence commands
items: nmap <host> — which ports answer (22/80/443 open)
dig <name> — ANSWER SECTION with the A record
ss — listening sockets
systemctl status <svc> — unit state
journalctl -u <svc> — service logs
sha256sum <file> — real SHA-256 identity
grep <pattern> <file> — search the record
ps — what is actually running

sections.heading: Graph vocabulary
items: node — any entity tracked in the model (user, host, IP, domain, file hash, vulnerability)
edge — a labeled relationship between two nodes (logged into, resolved to, downloaded)
degree — number of edges on a node; high-degree nodes are attacker highways
centrality — how much traffic or how many paths flow through a node
directed edge — a relationship with a direction (A downloaded FROM B)
security graph — the living model of your whole environment as nodes and edges
attack graph — the subgraph of exploitable paths to your targets
knowledge graph — threat-intel indicators linked to campaigns and actors

sections.heading: Attack-graph playbook
items: inventory first — you cannot graph what you have not discovered
model flaws AND misconfigs as exploit edges
compute shortest paths to the crown jewels
find the choke point (highest betweenness on those paths)
break the path: patch, segment, or remove the edge
re-scan and re-run the graph to prove the path is gone
never trust yesterday's graph — redeployments redraw the map

sections.heading: Zero Trust + graphs
items: never trust, always verify — re-evaluate every access decision
assume breach — treat unexpected edges as hostile until proven otherwise
microsegmentation — allow-list approved edges, alert on new ones
ReBAC — policies are path queries on the identity graph
continuous verification — device/location/behavior edges change, trust follows
anomalous edge — a first-seen connection between strangers is the classic signal

sections.heading: ML detection vocabulary
items: Supervised learning — learns from labeled examples; strong on known threats, blind to novel ones
Unsupervised learning — finds structure without labels; clustering and dimensionality reduction
Anomaly detection — models 'normal' and flags deviations; the workhorse for novel threats
UEBA — user and entity behavior analytics: per-user baselines plus peer-group comparison
Feature engineering — encoding raw logs into model inputs (login velocity, rare processes, domain entropy)
Concept drift — model decay as attacker behavior and legitimate traffic shift over time

sections.heading: Detection metrics
items: Precision — of all flagged alerts, how many were real
Recall — of all real attacks, how many were flagged
Threshold tuning — sliding the decision cutoff trades precision against recall
Alert fatigue — when false positives train analysts to ignore the queue
DGA — domain generation algorithm; detected via character entropy of domain names

sections.heading: Agent and LLM security
items: Direct prompt injection — attacker input overrides app instructions (OWASP LLM01:2025, the #1 LLM risk)
Indirect prompt injection — hidden instructions inside retrieved data (email, web, docs)
Jailbreak — defeating the model's own safety policy; distinct from hijacking app behavior
Tool poisoning — malicious tool descriptions or metadata steer an agent to misuse its tools (MCP ecosystem risk)
Insecure output handling — executing or trusting model output without validation
Least-privilege tools — grant each tool only the scope its task requires

sections.heading: Adversarial ML and governance
items: Evasion — perturbing inputs at inference time to dodge a classifier
Poisoning — corrupting training data to corrupt the model
Extraction — querying a model to steal its behavior or parameters
MITRE ATLAS — knowledge base of adversarial ML tactics and techniques
Red-teaming and evals — adversarial testing of AI systems before deployment
Human-in-the-loop — required approval for high-impact or irreversible agent actions
SOAR — security orchestration, automation and response; automate enrichment, gate containment

glossary.def: Default-deny execution control: only explicitly approved applications, scripts, and installers may run.
Default-allow model: everything runs except recognized-bad items — the window zero-days live in.
Deny-by-default posture: unknown code, devices, or connections are refused unless explicitly approved.
Containment applied on top of allowlisting; restricts what a permitted app may do across app-to-app, file, registry, and network dimensions.
Agent mode that catalogs applications and dependencies and auto-builds policies before enforcement; temporarily disables file blocking.
Temporary mode that pauses file blocking for installs — must be tightly scoped and time-boxed.
Grants specific approved applications admin rights for standard users — just-in-time, per-app, time-boxed — without standing admin rights.
An elevated or trusted process spawning another tool (e.g., PowerShell) to inherit its privileges — countered by ringfencing the elevated process.
Device and path policy: USB approved by serial, user, file type, time, and encryption; unapproved devices do not connect.
Centrally managed host firewall; rules by port, source IP, and dynamic ACLs; egress allowlisting pins apps to approved destinations.
Zero Trust Network Access: per-session, per-application brokered connections (commonly over port 443) with no open inbound ports — deny-by-default for network access.
Portal queue where end-user software requests arrive for admin review and decision.
Real-time audit showing what was allowed or denied across endpoints — and why; the evidence layer for triage.
One-button cloud VDI sandbox launched from an approval request; logs AV flags, canary-file access, and registry/system changes.
24/7/365 US-based managed detection and response team; validates alerts, isolates hosts, acts on customer runbooks; ~60-second average response.
Design and operate as if the attacker already has a foothold — least privilege, containment, and monitoring everywhere.
Attacks that hijack trusted built-in tools (Word, PowerShell) instead of dropping malware — defeated by behavior containment, not signatures.
Scoped, ticketed, tested changes with validation and rollback — emergency speed never cancels the process.
A node in an attack graph representing a system or weakness, connected by edges that represent steps an attacker could take between them.
How central a node is to paths through the graph (for example, betweenness: how many shortest paths cross it).
The most valuable assets in the environment (customer data, finance systems, source code): what attack paths are measured against.
A labeled connection between two nodes, representing a relationship such as 'logged into' or 'resolved to'.
A graph of threat indicators (IPs, domains, hashes) linked to campaigns, actors, and each other through shared infrastructure.
The practice of mapping relationships in data to reveal hidden associations; rooted in Euler's 1736 graph theory, 1970s paper link charts, and post-2001 intelligence work.
A segment of the network so small that its allowed communications can be enumerated as a graph of approved edges.
An entity in the graph: a user, host, IP address, domain, file, or vulnerability.
Access control where policy is evaluated by traversing relationships on a graph (for example: user reports_to manager who owns the resource's project).
A machine-learning model that operates directly on graph structure to classify nodes or subgraphs, for example labeling attack vs normal behavior.
Monitoring user and entity behavior by modeling their normal relationship patterns and flagging structural anomalies.
ML trained on labeled examples; classifies new inputs into known categories.
ML approach that models normal behavior and flags statistically rare deviations.
Turning raw telemetry into numeric model inputs, e.g. login velocity or domain entropy.
Share of flagged alerts that were real; the false-positive economics of the queue.
Share of real attacks the detector flagged; the miss rate's complement.
Decay of model performance as the data distribution shifts over time.
Attacker-crafted instructions that override an LLM application's intended behavior; direct (user input) or indirect (retrieved data).
Crafted input that defeats an LLM's own safety policy or refusal behavior.
Malicious tool descriptions or metadata that manipulate an AI agent into misusing its tools.
Failing to validate LLM output before acting on it, e.g. executing generated commands.
Adversarial ML technique: perturbing inputs to cross a classifier's decision boundary.
Adversarial Threat Landscape for AI Systems; MITRE's knowledge base of AI attack tactics.
Security orchestration, automation and response; playbooks that enrich automatically and gate containment on humans.
Required human approval before high-impact or irreversible automated actions.
